title: Quality Sleep Is the Brain's Best Defense, Neurologists Warn on World Brain Day
excerpt: New research links sleep duration to Alzheimer's biomarkers while Indian doctors flag screen-driven sleep deprivation as a growing threat to brain health.
body:
• A UT Health San Antonio study of 2,410 people found that regularly sleeping 8.5 or more hours is associated with higher levels of an Alzheimer's-related protein (p-tau181) in the blood, with the sharpest rise beyond 10 hours.
  • Indian neurologists warn that screen addiction across all age groups is disrupting sleep patterns, raising the risk of stroke, dementia, and mood disorders.
  • World Brain Day 2026, themed "Brain Health: Access for All," highlights that over 3.4 billion people globally live with neurological conditions, with India bearing a disproportionate stroke burden.
  • Experts recommend at least seven hours of consistent nightly sleep, limited screen use before bed, regular exercise, and blood pressure monitoring as key protective measures.

On World Brain Day, marked annually on July 22, neurologists and researchers are raising the alarm on a deceptively simple threat to brain health: poor sleep. New research from UT Health San Antonio has found that both too little and too much sleep are associated with elevated Alzheimer's-related proteins in the blood, while Indian neurologists warn that screen addiction is eroding sleep quality across all age groups — increasing the risk of stroke, dementia, and cognitive decline.

New Study Links Oversleeping to Alzheimer's Biomarker

A study published in May 2026 in Alzheimer's & Dementia, the journal of the Alzheimer's Association, analyzed 2,410 participants from the long-running Framingham Heart Study. Researchers at UT Health San Antonio's Glenn Biggs Institute for Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases found that regularly sleeping eight-and-a-half hours or more per night was linked to higher levels of phosphorylated tau 181 (p-tau181), a blood-based biomarker that is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. The association grew sharply beyond 10 hours of nightly sleep.

"A lot of people worry about whether their sleep habits are affecting their brain health. Because this is a snapshot in time rather than a long-term study, we cannot say that long sleep causes Alzheimer's, but the findings suggest it may be worth monitoring, and that more sleep is not always better for brain health."

— Dr. Vanessa M. Young, Postdoctoral Research Fellow, Glenn Biggs Institute, UT Health San Antonio

The study used non-linear modeling techniques — restricted cubic splines — to uncover the relationship. "When you force a straight line through data that curves, you miss the story entirely," Young said. The link held after adjusting for age, sex, sleep apnea, depression, kidney function, and the APOE ε4 genotype, a common genetic variant tied to late-onset Alzheimer's risk. The researchers concluded that long sleep may serve as "a potential behavioral marker of elevated p-tau181."

Screen Addiction Eroding Sleep Quality in India

The study's findings arrive as Indian doctors raise alarm about the country's worsening sleep habits. Writing in The Week on World Brain Day, the president of the Indian Stroke Association warned that screen addiction has become rampant across all age groups. "Somewhere along the way, sleep stopped being an important biological necessity and became the first thing to be sacrificed," the op-ed noted.

During deep sleep, the brain's glymphatic system clears away toxins accumulated during waking hours and strengthens neural pathways critical for memory and learning, according to the Cleveland Clinic. When this process is consistently disrupted, the consequences extend well beyond fatigue — chronically poor sleep raises the risk of high blood pressure, stroke, and dementia.

India carries a heavy share of this burden. The country accounts for roughly 10 percent of the global stroke burden, with a stroke occurring every 30 seconds, according to Sakra World Hospital. A Lancet study found that stroke accounts for nearly 38 percent of all neurological disorder disability in India, with states such as West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, and Tripura bearing the highest rates.

"People think that using their phone less will keep them safe from health problems caused by screens. That is not the whole truth. At work we are around laptops and desktops for a time and even the light in the room can affect our body's natural clock."

— Dr. Neha Kapoor, Associate Director and Head of Neurology, Asian Hospital

Implications for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad, the convergence of lifestyle factors — long work hours, heavy reliance on screens, and disrupted sleep schedules — makes these findings directly relevant. Jet lag from frequent trips to India, shift work common in healthcare and IT sectors, and the stress of maintaining family connections across time zones can all compromise sleep quality. The UT San Antonio study adds a new wrinkle: sleeping more on weekends to "catch up" may not be the protective measure many assume.

What's Next

World Brain Day 2026, organized by the World Federation of Neurology under the theme "Brain Health: Access for All," underscores that more than 3.4 billion people globally live with neurological conditions, making brain disorders the leading cause of disability worldwide. The campaign calls for closing gaps in diagnosis, specialist access, and treatment.

For individuals, the protective steps remain straightforward: maintain a consistent sleep schedule of at least seven hours nightly, limit screen exposure at least two hours before bedtime, exercise four to five days a week, eat a nutritious diet, manage stress deliberately, and keep blood pressure in check. Neurologists urge people not to dismiss warning signs — sudden severe headaches, numbness, face drooping, slurred speech, or unexplained vision changes — as mere tiredness.

"Brain health should not be something we think about only in hindsight, because more than any other organ, the brain rarely gives a second chance to those who ignored the initial warnings," wrote the Indian Stroke Association president.
nri_angle: Long work hours, screen-heavy jobs, frequent India travel, and cross-timezone family communication make sleep disruption a particular risk for the Indian diaspora.
